clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AAAS gene (chromosome 12q13) encoding the nucleoporin ALADIN.
Classic triad: alacrima (deficient tear production), achalasia of the cardia, and adrenocorticotrophin-resistant adrenal insufficiency.
Alacrima is usually the earliest and most consistent feature, often present from infancy, and may precede other manifestations by years.
Adrenal insufficiency is characteristically an isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, with mineralocorticoid function often preserved initially but able to fail later.
Achalasia produces dysphagia, regurgitation, recurrent chest infections and failure to thrive, and may present with hypoglycaemia-related collapse when combined with cortisol deficiency.

Progressive neurological involvement (autonomic dysfunction, sensorimotor polyneuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, dysarthria and mild cognitive impairment) leads to the broader '4A' description with autonomic dysfunction.
Reduced tear production can be demonstrated at the bedside with a Schirmer test.
Consider the diagnosis in any child with unexplained adrenal insufficiency, hypoglycaemic seizures or early-onset achalasia.
reference.pathophysiology: The AAAS gene on chromosome 12q13 encodes ALADIN, a WD-repeat protein that is a component of the nuclear pore complex. Pathogenic variants mislocalise ALADIN away from the nuclear envelope and impair nucleocytoplasmic transport, particularly of proteins involved in DNA repair and defence against oxidative stress, rendering neuroendocrine, neuronal and exocrine tissues selectively vulnerable. In the adrenal cortex the zona fasciculata becomes resistant to adrenocorticotrophin stimulation, producing glucocorticoid deficiency; degeneration of lacrimal gland function produces alacrima; and progressive loss of oesophageal myenteric plexus neurons produces achalasia with failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. A slowly progressive neurodegenerative process affects autonomic, sensory and motor pathways as well as the optic nerves, accounting for the multisystem and evolving nature of the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency (MC2R or MRAP mutations)
Autoimmune adrenalitis and autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes
Sjogren syndrome and other causes of keratoconjunctivitis sicca
additionalInvestigations: Morning serum cortisol with adrenocorticotrophin (short cosyntropin) stimulation demonstrating a subnormal cortisol response
Plasma adrenocorticotrophin (markedly raised) with renin and aldosterone to assess the mineralocorticoid axis
Schirmer test and ophthalmology review for alacrima and keratoconjunctivitis
Oesophageal manometry (absent peristalsis, non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter) and barium swallow
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude pseudoachalasia and mucosal disease
Nerve conduction studies and autonomic function testing to characterise neurological involvement
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, collapse or seizures, which may be the presenting event and is life-threatening
Hypoglycaemic seizures in an infant or young child
Autonomic instability with postural symptoms and cardiovascular lability
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable: the life-threatening adrenal insufficiency is manageable with glucocorticoid replacement and achalasia is treatable, but the neurodegenerative features are progressive and represent the principal long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing isolated dry eyes or alacrima to benign causes and missing the underlying syndrome.
Failing to screen for adrenal insufficiency, a preventable cause of sudden death.
Assuming mineralocorticoid function is always intact, as it can decline over time.
Overlooking the diagnosis in adults, in whom presentation may be delayed and incomplete.
Misdiagnosing achalasia-related respiratory symptoms as asthma or recurrent chest infection.
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease (standard reference)
